case_info.scenario: A man in his 30s presented with an approximately 6-month history of asymptomatic plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet. He had no relevant medical history or any known inciting factors. Physical examination demonstrated thick yellow to brown plaques overlying the interphalangeal joints of both first digits of the feet (Figure, A). A combination of urea cream, 20%, and clobetasol ointment, 0.05%, applied twice daily to the affected area for approximately 4 weeks yielded no improvement. At a follow-up visit, a tangential shave biopsy specimen was taken from the right dorsal first digit toe (Figure, B).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of yellow-brown plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet, with prominent scale and a healing biopsy site on the right great toe. Plaques are centered on the interphalangeal joint, potentially an area of high friction. B, Histopathologic examination showed large cells with small, round, dark blue central nuclei and abundant light pink cytoplasm scattered within the epidermis.
case_info.explanation: The shave biopsy findings revealed numerous keratinocytes with abundant pink cytoplasm, scattered at all levels of the epidermis. These scattered keratinocytes had small, round, pyknotic, blue nuclei with perinuclear clearing and abundant light pink cytoplasm; the histopathologic features were those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. Pagetoid dyskeratosis can be an incidental microscopic finding but has been described as a histopathologic feature in biopsy specimens of orange-brown plaques or hyperpigmented macules from the hands.1Trauma may be an inciting factor. The toe lesions in this patient with pagetoid dyskeratosis were likely analogous to pagetoid dyskeratosis of the hands. Pagetoid dyskeratosis, which was originally thought to be an artifact of processing, is a pattern of reactive premature keratinization that is often considered secondary to trauma or friction; however, its pathophysiologic mechanisms are not completely understood.2A unique feature of pagetoid dyskeratosis is that it is often associated with orthokeratosis rather than parakeratosis, and intercellular bridges with other keratinocytes are maintained.2,3This is in contrast to most dyskeratotic processes, which have dyskeratotic cells showing dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and overlying parakeratosis.3The pattern of pagetoid dyskeratosis can also be incidentally seen in the epidermis of melanocytic nevi, acrochordons, and fibromas, even in the absence of any inciting trauma.3Body sites that are most susceptible to rubbing or friction, such as the axillary region, head, and trunk, show the highest incidence of pagetoid dyskeratosis, which supports the hypothesis of an association with a friction-induced mechanism.2,3Most cases of pagetoid dyskeratosis are self-limiting, without further treatment needed. However, a few case reports indicate that lesions were treated with keratolytics, such as urea- or lactic acid−based creams or cryotherapy, with limited success.4 Although pagetoid dyskeratosis itself is a benign finding, neoplasia must be ruled out. Pagetoid Bowen disease can present clinically as a slow-growing variably pigmented plaque or scaly lesion, often in areas with sun exposure. Under histopathologic examination, the epidermis shows enlarged atypical keratinocytes scattered at all levels of the epidermis, with interspersed mitoses.5The stratum corneum often shows alternating patterns of orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, and dyskeratotic cells are also present. There is a tinctorial difference between atypical cells and surrounding normal keratinocytes.5 Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is an autosomal recessive or acquired condition that is associated with β−human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Lesions vary in appearance, ranging from multiple flat papules resembling verruca plana to pityriasiform, thin plaques, and brown macules; lesions are commonly on the face or distal extremities.6Histopathologically, the epidermis is acanthotic and hyperkeratotic, with an irregular granular layer. The cells have perinuclear halos with blue-gray pale cytoplasm.6EV cells differ greatly morphologically from those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. If testing for HPV is performed (not required for either diagnosis), HPV can be detected in EV but not in pagetoid dyskeratosis. Human polyomaviruses 6 and 7, which are chronically shed from the skin, can cause pruritus and skin thickening in individuals who are immunocompromised. Histopathologic findings include dyskeratotic cells in the epidermis and parakeratotic cells with pink cytoplasm in layers within the stratum corneum, resembling peacock plumage.7 In summary, pagetoid dyskeratosis can be the characteristic microscopic finding in yellow-brown plaques on acral surfaces. Although its exact pathomechanism is unknown, this type of clinical presentation with pagetoid dyskeratosis may be secondary to chronic friction.

dialogue_history.text: Based on the clinical presentation of yellow-brown plaques with histopathological findings of large cells and the distribution pattern over interphalangeal joints, the most appropriate next step in management is to consider Bowen disease (A). This condition can present as squamous cell carcinoma in situ, particularly in areas prone to friction and irritation. Given the lack of response to topical therapies, further evaluation for malignancy through excisional biopsy or closer surveillance may be warranted.

dialogue_history.speaker: medical
dialogue_history.text: I agree that Bowen disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ) is a strong consideration given the yellow-brown plaques, location, and lack of response to topical therapy. However, the large cells seen on histopathology are not typical for Bowen disease, which usually shows full-thickness epidermal atypia and mitoses. A more likely diagnosis given the clinical and histologic picture is knuckle pads, which are benign fibromatous plaques over joints and show dermal fibroplasia with large fibroblasts, not malignancy.

case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of yellow-brown plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet, with prominent scale and a healing biopsy site on the right great toe. Plaques are centered on the interphalangeal joint, potentially an area of high friction. B, Histopathologic examination showed large cells with small, round, dark blue central nuclei and abundant light pink cytoplasm scattered within the epidermis.
case_info.explanation: The shave biopsy findings revealed numerous keratinocytes with abundant pink cytoplasm, scattered at all levels of the epidermis. These scattered keratinocytes had small, round, pyknotic, blue nuclei with perinuclear clearing and abundant light pink cytoplasm; the histopathologic features were those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. Pagetoid dyskeratosis can be an incidental microscopic finding but has been described as a histopathologic feature in biopsy specimens of orange-brown plaques or hyperpigmented macules from the hands.1Trauma may be an inciting factor. The toe lesions in this patient with pagetoid dyskeratosis were likely analogous to pagetoid dyskeratosis of the hands. Pagetoid dyskeratosis, which was originally thought to be an artifact of processing, is a pattern of reactive premature keratinization that is often considered secondary to trauma or friction; however, its pathophysiologic mechanisms are not completely understood.2A unique feature of pagetoid dyskeratosis is that it is often associated with orthokeratosis rather than parakeratosis, and intercellular bridges with other keratinocytes are maintained.2,3This is in contrast to most dyskeratotic processes, which have dyskeratotic cells showing dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and overlying parakeratosis.3The pattern of pagetoid dyskeratosis can also be incidentally seen in the epidermis of melanocytic nevi, acrochordons, and fibromas, even in the absence of any inciting trauma.3Body sites that are most susceptible to rubbing or friction, such as the axillary region, head, and trunk, show the highest incidence of pagetoid dyskeratosis, which supports the hypothesis of an association with a friction-induced mechanism.2,3Most cases of pagetoid dyskeratosis are self-limiting, without further treatment needed. However, a few case reports indicate that lesions were treated with keratolytics, such as urea- or lactic acid−based creams or cryotherapy, with limited success.4 Although pagetoid dyskeratosis itself is a benign finding, neoplasia must be ruled out. Pagetoid Bowen disease can present clinically as a slow-growing variably pigmented plaque or scaly lesion, often in areas with sun exposure. Under histopathologic examination, the epidermis shows enlarged atypical keratinocytes scattered at all levels of the epidermis, with interspersed mitoses.5The stratum corneum often shows alternating patterns of orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, and dyskeratotic cells are also present. There is a tinctorial difference between atypical cells and surrounding normal keratinocytes.5 Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is an autosomal recessive or acquired condition that is associated with β−human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Lesions vary in appearance, ranging from multiple flat papules resembling verruca plana to pityriasiform, thin plaques, and brown macules; lesions are commonly on the face or distal extremities.6Histopathologically, the epidermis is acanthotic and hyperkeratotic, with an irregular granular layer. The cells have perinuclear halos with blue-gray pale cytoplasm.6EV cells differ greatly morphologically from those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. If testing for HPV is performed (not required for either diagnosis), HPV can be detected in EV but not in pagetoid dyskeratosis. Human polyomaviruses 6 and 7, which are chronically shed from the skin, can cause pruritus and skin thickening in individuals who are immunocompromised. Histopathologic findings include dyskeratotic cells in the epidermis and parakeratotic cells with pink cytoplasm in layers within the stratum corneum, resembling peacock plumage.7 In summary, pagetoid dyskeratosis can be the characteristic microscopic finding in yellow-brown plaques on acral surfaces. Although its exact pathomechanism is unknown, this type of clinical presentation with pagetoid dyskeratosis may be secondary to chronic friction.

case_info.explanation: The shave biopsy findings revealed numerous keratinocytes with abundant pink cytoplasm, scattered at all levels of the epidermis. These scattered keratinocytes had small, round, pyknotic, blue nuclei with perinuclear clearing and abundant light pink cytoplasm; the histopathologic features were those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. Pagetoid dyskeratosis can be an incidental microscopic finding but has been described as a histopathologic feature in biopsy specimens of orange-brown plaques or hyperpigmented macules from the hands.1Trauma may be an inciting factor. The toe lesions in this patient with pagetoid dyskeratosis were likely analogous to pagetoid dyskeratosis of the hands. Pagetoid dyskeratosis, which was originally thought to be an artifact of processing, is a pattern of reactive premature keratinization that is often considered secondary to trauma or friction; however, its pathophysiologic mechanisms are not completely understood.2A unique feature of pagetoid dyskeratosis is that it is often associated with orthokeratosis rather than parakeratosis, and intercellular bridges with other keratinocytes are maintained.2,3This is in contrast to most dyskeratotic processes, which have dyskeratotic cells showing dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and overlying parakeratosis.3The pattern of pagetoid dyskeratosis can also be incidentally seen in the epidermis of melanocytic nevi, acrochordons, and fibromas, even in the absence of any inciting trauma.3Body sites that are most susceptible to rubbing or friction, such as the axillary region, head, and trunk, show the highest incidence of pagetoid dyskeratosis, which supports the hypothesis of an association with a friction-induced mechanism.2,3Most cases of pagetoid dyskeratosis are self-limiting, without further treatment needed. However, a few case reports indicate that lesions were treated with keratolytics, such as urea- or lactic acid−based creams or cryotherapy, with limited success.4 Although pagetoid dyskeratosis itself is a benign finding, neoplasia must be ruled out. Pagetoid Bowen disease can present clinically as a slow-growing variably pigmented plaque or scaly lesion, often in areas with sun exposure. Under histopathologic examination, the epidermis shows enlarged atypical keratinocytes scattered at all levels of the epidermis, with interspersed mitoses.5The stratum corneum often shows alternating patterns of orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, and dyskeratotic cells are also present. There is a tinctorial difference between atypical cells and surrounding normal keratinocytes.5 Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is an autosomal recessive or acquired condition that is associated with β−human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Lesions vary in appearance, ranging from multiple flat papules resembling verruca plana to pityriasiform, thin plaques, and brown macules; lesions are commonly on the face or distal extremities.6Histopathologically, the epidermis is acanthotic and hyperkeratotic, with an irregular granular layer. The cells have perinuclear halos with blue-gray pale cytoplasm.6EV cells differ greatly morphologically from those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. If testing for HPV is performed (not required for either diagnosis), HPV can be detected in EV but not in pagetoid dyskeratosis. Human polyomaviruses 6 and 7, which are chronically shed from the skin, can cause pruritus and skin thickening in individuals who are immunocompromised. Histopathologic findings include dyskeratotic cells in the epidermis and parakeratotic cells with pink cytoplasm in layers within the stratum corneum, resembling peacock plumage.7 In summary, pagetoid dyskeratosis can be the characteristic microscopic finding in yellow-brown plaques on acral surfaces. Although its exact pathomechanism is unknown, this type of clinical presentation with pagetoid dyskeratosis may be secondary to chronic friction.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.

case_info.explanation: The shave biopsy findings revealed numerous keratinocytes with abundant pink cytoplasm, scattered at all levels of the epidermis. These scattered keratinocytes had small, round, pyknotic, blue nuclei with perinuclear clearing and abundant light pink cytoplasm; the histopathologic features were those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. Pagetoid dyskeratosis can be an incidental microscopic finding but has been described as a histopathologic feature in biopsy specimens of orange-brown plaques or hyperpigmented macules from the hands.1Trauma may be an inciting factor. The toe lesions in this patient with pagetoid dyskeratosis were likely analogous to pagetoid dyskeratosis of the hands. Pagetoid dyskeratosis, which was originally thought to be an artifact of processing, is a pattern of reactive premature keratinization that is often considered secondary to trauma or friction; however, its pathophysiologic mechanisms are not completely understood.2A unique feature of pagetoid dyskeratosis is that it is often associated with orthokeratosis rather than parakeratosis, and intercellular bridges with other keratinocytes are maintained.2,3This is in contrast to most dyskeratotic processes, which have dyskeratotic cells showing dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and overlying parakeratosis.3The pattern of pagetoid dyskeratosis can also be incidentally seen in the epidermis of melanocytic nevi, acrochordons, and fibromas, even in the absence of any inciting trauma.3Body sites that are most susceptible to rubbing or friction, such as the axillary region, head, and trunk, show the highest incidence of pagetoid dyskeratosis, which supports the hypothesis of an association with a friction-induced mechanism.2,3Most cases of pagetoid dyskeratosis are self-limiting, without further treatment needed. However, a few case reports indicate that lesions were treated with keratolytics, such as urea- or lactic acid−based creams or cryotherapy, with limited success.4 Although pagetoid dyskeratosis itself is a benign finding, neoplasia must be ruled out. Pagetoid Bowen disease can present clinically as a slow-growing variably pigmented plaque or scaly lesion, often in areas with sun exposure. Under histopathologic examination, the epidermis shows enlarged atypical keratinocytes scattered at all levels of the epidermis, with interspersed mitoses.5The stratum corneum often shows alternating patterns of orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, and dyskeratotic cells are also present. There is a tinctorial difference between atypical cells and surrounding normal keratinocytes.5 Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is an autosomal recessive or acquired condition that is associated with β−human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Lesions vary in appearance, ranging from multiple flat papules resembling verruca plana to pityriasiform, thin plaques, and brown macules; lesions are commonly on the face or distal extremities.6Histopathologically, the epidermis is acanthotic and hyperkeratotic, with an irregular granular layer. The cells have perinuclear halos with blue-gray pale cytoplasm.6EV cells differ greatly morphologically from those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. If testing for HPV is performed (not required for either diagnosis), HPV can be detected in EV but not in pagetoid dyskeratosis. Human polyomaviruses 6 and 7, which are chronically shed from the skin, can cause pruritus and skin thickening in individuals who are immunocompromised. Histopathologic findings include dyskeratotic cells in the epidermis and parakeratotic cells with pink cytoplasm in layers within the stratum corneum, resembling peacock plumage.7 In summary, pagetoid dyskeratosis can be the characteristic microscopic finding in yellow-brown plaques on acral surfaces. Although its exact pathomechanism is unknown, this type of clinical presentation with pagetoid dyskeratosis may be secondary to chronic friction.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

case_info.explanation: The shave biopsy findings revealed numerous keratinocytes with abundant pink cytoplasm, scattered at all levels of the epidermis. These scattered keratinocytes had small, round, pyknotic, blue nuclei with perinuclear clearing and abundant light pink cytoplasm; the histopathologic features were those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. Pagetoid dyskeratosis can be an incidental microscopic finding but has been described as a histopathologic feature in biopsy specimens of orange-brown plaques or hyperpigmented macules from the hands.1Trauma may be an inciting factor. The toe lesions in this patient with pagetoid dyskeratosis were likely analogous to pagetoid dyskeratosis of the hands. Pagetoid dyskeratosis, which was originally thought to be an artifact of processing, is a pattern of reactive premature keratinization that is often considered secondary to trauma or friction; however, its pathophysiologic mechanisms are not completely understood.2A unique feature of pagetoid dyskeratosis is that it is often associated with orthokeratosis rather than parakeratosis, and intercellular bridges with other keratinocytes are maintained.2,3This is in contrast to most dyskeratotic processes, which have dyskeratotic cells showing dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and overlying parakeratosis.3The pattern of pagetoid dyskeratosis can also be incidentally seen in the epidermis of melanocytic nevi, acrochordons, and fibromas, even in the absence of any inciting trauma.3Body sites that are most susceptible to rubbing or friction, such as the axillary region, head, and trunk, show the highest incidence of pagetoid dyskeratosis, which supports the hypothesis of an association with a friction-induced mechanism.2,3Most cases of pagetoid dyskeratosis are self-limiting, without further treatment needed. However, a few case reports indicate that lesions were treated with keratolytics, such as urea- or lactic acid−based creams or cryotherapy, with limited success.4 Although pagetoid dyskeratosis itself is a benign finding, neoplasia must be ruled out. Pagetoid Bowen disease can present clinically as a slow-growing variably pigmented plaque or scaly lesion, often in areas with sun exposure. Under histopathologic examination, the epidermis shows enlarged atypical keratinocytes scattered at all levels of the epidermis, with interspersed mitoses.5The stratum corneum often shows alternating patterns of orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, and dyskeratotic cells are also present. There is a tinctorial difference between atypical cells and surrounding normal keratinocytes.5 Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is an autosomal recessive or acquired condition that is associated with β−human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Lesions vary in appearance, ranging from multiple flat papules resembling verruca plana to pityriasiform, thin plaques, and brown macules; lesions are commonly on the face or distal extremities.6Histopathologically, the epidermis is acanthotic and hyperkeratotic, with an irregular granular layer. The cells have perinuclear halos with blue-gray pale cytoplasm.6EV cells differ greatly morphologically from those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. If testing for HPV is performed (not required for either diagnosis), HPV can be detected in EV but not in pagetoid dyskeratosis. Human polyomaviruses 6 and 7, which are chronically shed from the skin, can cause pruritus and skin thickening in individuals who are immunocompromised. Histopathologic findings include dyskeratotic cells in the epidermis and parakeratotic cells with pink cytoplasm in layers within the stratum corneum, resembling peacock plumage.7 In summary, pagetoid dyskeratosis can be the characteristic microscopic finding in yellow-brown plaques on acral surfaces. Although its exact pathomechanism is unknown, this type of clinical presentation with pagetoid dyskeratosis may be secondary to chronic friction.

case_info.explanation: The shave biopsy findings revealed numerous keratinocytes with abundant pink cytoplasm, scattered at all levels of the epidermis. These scattered keratinocytes had small, round, pyknotic, blue nuclei with perinuclear clearing and abundant light pink cytoplasm; the histopathologic features were those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. Human polyomaviruses 6 and 7, which are chronically shed from the skin, can cause pruritus and skin thickening in individuals who are immunocompromised. Histopathologic findings include dyskeratotic cells in the epidermis and parakeratotic cells with pink cytoplasm in layers within the stratum corneum, resembling peacock plumage.7 In summary, pagetoid dyskeratosis can be the characteristic microscopic finding in yellow-brown plaques on acral surfaces. case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of yellow-brown plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet, with prominent scale and a healing biopsy site on the right great toe. Plaques are centered on the interphalangeal joint, potentially an area of high friction. case_info.explanation: The shave biopsy findings revealed numerous keratinocytes with abundant pink cytoplasm, scattered at all levels of the epidermis. These scattered keratinocytes had small, round, pyknotic, blue nuclei with perinuclear clearing and abundant light pink cytoplasm; the histopathologic features were those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. Pagetoid dyskeratosis can be an incidental microscopic finding but has been described as a histopathologic feature in biopsy specimens of orange-brown plaques or hyperpigmented macules from the hands.1Trauma may be an inciting factor. The toe lesions in this patient with pagetoid dyskeratosis were likely analogous to pagetoid dyskeratosis of the hands. Pagetoid dyskeratosis, which was originally thought to be an artifact of processing, is a pattern of reactive premature keratinization that is often considered secondary to trauma or friction; however, its pathophysiologic mechanisms are not completely understood.2A unique feature of pagetoid dyskeratosis is that it is often associated with orthokeratosis rather than parakeratosis, and intercellular bridges with other keratinocytes are maintained.2,3This is in contrast to most dyskeratotic processes, which have dyskeratotic cells showing dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and overlying parakeratosis.3The pattern of pagetoid dyskeratosis can also be incidentally seen in the epidermis of melanocytic nevi, acrochordons, and fibromas, even in the absence of any inciting trauma.3Body sites that are most susceptible to rubbing or friction, such as the axillary region, head, and trunk, show the highest incidence of pagetoid dyskeratosis, which supports the hypothesis of an association with a friction-induced mechanism.2,3Most cases of pagetoid dyskeratosis are self-limiting, without further treatment needed. However, a few case reports indicate that lesions were treated with keratolytics, such as urea- or lactic acid−based creams or cryotherapy, with limited success.4 Although pagetoid dyskeratosis itself is a benign finding, neoplasia must be ruled out. Pagetoid Bowen disease can present clinically as a slow-growing variably pigmented plaque or scaly lesion, often in areas with sun exposure. Under histopathologic examination, the epidermis shows enlarged atypical keratinocytes scattered at all levels of the epidermis, with interspersed mitoses.5The stratum corneum often shows alternating patterns of orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, and dyskeratotic cells are also present. There is a tinctorial difference between atypical cells and surrounding normal keratinocytes.5 Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is an autosomal recessive or acquired condition that is associated with β−human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Lesions vary in appearance, ranging from multiple flat papules resembling verruca plana to pityriasiform, thin plaques, and brown macules; lesions are commonly on the face or distal extremities.6Histopathologically, the epidermis is acanthotic and hyperkeratotic, with an irregular granular layer. The cells have perinuclear halos with blue-gray pale cytoplasm.6EV cells differ greatly morphologically from those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. If testing for HPV is performed (not required for either diagnosis), HPV can be detected in EV but not in pagetoid dyskeratosis. Human polyomaviruses 6 and 7, which are chronically shed from the skin, can cause pruritus and skin thickening in individuals who are immunocompromised. Histopathologic findings include dyskeratotic cells in the epidermis and parakeratotic cells with pink cytoplasm in layers within the stratum corneum, resembling peacock plumage.7 In summary, pagetoid dyskeratosis can be the characteristic microscopic finding in yellow-brown plaques on acral surfaces. Although its exact pathomechanism is unknown, this type of clinical presentation with pagetoid dyskeratosis may be secondary to chronic friction.

case_info.explanation: The shave biopsy findings revealed numerous keratinocytes with abundant pink cytoplasm, scattered at all levels of the epidermis. These scattered keratinocytes had small, round, pyknotic, blue nuclei with perinuclear clearing and abundant light pink cytoplasm; the histopathologic features were those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. Pagetoid dyskeratosis can be an incidental microscopic finding but has been described as a histopathologic feature in biopsy specimens of orange-brown plaques or hyperpigmented macules from the hands.1Trauma may be an inciting factor. The toe lesions in this patient with pagetoid dyskeratosis were likely analogous to pagetoid dyskeratosis of the hands. Pagetoid dyskeratosis, which was originally thought to be an artifact of processing, is a pattern of reactive premature keratinization that is often considered secondary to trauma or friction; however, its pathophysiologic mechanisms are not completely understood.2A unique feature of pagetoid dyskeratosis is that it is often associated with orthokeratosis rather than parakeratosis, and intercellular bridges with other keratinocytes are maintained.2,3This is in contrast to most dyskeratotic processes, which have dyskeratotic cells showing dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and overlying parakeratosis.3The pattern of pagetoid dyskeratosis can also be incidentally seen in the epidermis of melanocytic nevi, acrochordons, and fibromas, even in the absence of any inciting trauma.3Body sites that are most susceptible to rubbing or friction, such as the axillary region, head, and trunk, show the highest incidence of pagetoid dyskeratosis, which supports the hypothesis of an association with a friction-induced mechanism.2,3Most cases of pagetoid dyskeratosis are self-limiting, without further treatment needed. However, a few case reports indicate that lesions were treated with keratolytics, such as urea- or lactic acid−based creams or cryotherapy, with limited success.4 Although pagetoid dyskeratosis itself is a benign finding, neoplasia must be ruled out. Pagetoid Bowen disease can present clinically as a slow-growing variably pigmented plaque or scaly lesion, often in areas with sun exposure. Under histopathologic examination, the epidermis shows enlarged atypical keratinocytes scattered at all levels of the epidermis, with interspersed mitoses.5The stratum corneum often shows alternating patterns of orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, and dyskeratotic cells are also present. There is a tinctorial difference between atypical cells and surrounding normal keratinocytes.5 Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is an autosomal recessive or acquired condition that is associated with β−human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Lesions vary in appearance, ranging from multiple flat papules resembling verruca plana to pityriasiform, thin plaques, and brown macules; lesions are commonly on the face or distal extremities.6Histopathologically, the epidermis is acanthotic and hyperkeratotic, with an irregular granular layer. The cells have perinuclear halos with blue-gray pale cytoplasm.6EV cells differ greatly morphologically from those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. If testing for HPV is performed (not required for either diagnosis), HPV can be detected in EV but not in pagetoid dyskeratosis. Human polyomaviruses 6 and 7, which are chronically shed from the skin, can cause pruritus and skin thickening in individuals who are immunocompromised. Histopathologic findings include dyskeratotic cells in the epidermis and parakeratotic cells with pink cytoplasm in layers within the stratum corneum, resembling peacock plumage.7 In summary, pagetoid dyskeratosis can be the characteristic microscopic finding in yellow-brown plaques on acral surfaces. Although its exact pathomechanism is unknown, this type of clinical presentation with pagetoid dyskeratosis may be secondary to chronic friction.
